headline: Alphabet's 13 percent one-day drop, despite Gemini 4 Carbon topping the Artificial Analysis index, dominated Moonshots' look at the week's AI market sell-off. Latent Space and The Cognitive Revolution focused on agents that run business work around the clock and how to keep them safe in production.

themes.title: Gemini 4 Carbon and Alphabet's sell-off
themes.body: Peter Diamandis reports that Gemini 4 Carbon scored 59 on the Artificial Analysis index, beating Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra, yet Alphabet shares fell 13 percent in a day, wiping out $500 billion despite 25 percent revenue growth. He blames slowing search ad revenue and 2026 capex of $195-205 billion. Dave Blundin argues Google's TPUs are now second only to Nvidia in compute manufactured.

themes.title: Agents that run the business
themes.body: Arca's Aman Singh tells Latent Space that at the AI-native wealth manager agents prompt people more than people prompt agents, running proactively around the clock. Per-client memory and a dreaming process let fresh agents pick up multi-day tasks. On The Cognitive Revolution, Union's Samvit Ramadurgam predicts many markets will soon be coordinated by agents, targeting 1 to 2 billion tokens per person per day.

themes.title: Keeping production agents safe
themes.body: Singh says Arca's safety restrictions are fully deterministic, every database write gets a fast LLM check, and outbound data passes PII rules plus a consensus of small models. Arena's Anastasios Angelopoulos argues that because models can tell when they are evaluated, alignment can only be measured in production; his index tracks unauthorized actions, false attributions and deceptive completions, and he says OpenAI leads Anthropic on all three.

themes.title: Memory as the inference bottleneck
themes.body: Kepler Computing's Debo Olaosebikan tells The Cognitive Revolution that most inference energy goes to fetching data from memory. Kepler replaces six transistors with one transistor and a ferroelectric capacitor, and he claims older-node fabs can then make chips better than advanced-node ones without EUV. On cost, Angelopoulos says Arena built a router after a simple thank-you cost $40 through cache invalidation.

themes.title: OpenAI's spending on math
themes.body: The Moonshots hosts discuss Sam Altman's remarks that OpenAI spent roughly $10 million on its Navier-Stokes proof and hundreds of millions on math overall, with an internal channel where staff threw their hardest problems at new models. Alexander Wissner-Gross speculates OpenAI may hold unpublished Millennium-problem results, and Diamandis predicts it will buy a launch company such as Rocket Lab.

whyItMatters: Agents that act proactively on client data need deterministic controls, verification on every write and production-based monitoring, while investor reaction to Alphabet's capex shows that AI infrastructure spending is now judged against slowing core revenue.
